Dermatology · published research

Psoriasis

Small randomized studies found short-term improvement in selected psoriasis plaques treated with blue or red visible light, with one comparison favoring more sustained erythema improvement under blue light. These findings do not establish durable remission or systemic disease control.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small randomized studies found short-term improvement in selected psoriasis plaques treated with blue or red visible light, with one comparison favoring more sustained erythema improvement under blue light. These findings do not establish durable remission or systemic disease control.

Summary of the Evidence

Nine publications are relevant to psoriasis: eight exact-category records and one mapped psoriasis-like skin-model study. The set includes four human primary reports, two reviews, two mouse-inclusive studies, and two laboratory reports, with one publication contributing to both animal and in-vitro categories. The clinical evidence is small but includes two randomized within-person comparisons; there is no large multi-center clinical trial in this category.

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized study of 47 people with mild psoriasis, blue visible light at 453 nm was applied to selected plaques while comparison plaques were left untreated. Both tested intensities produced reductions in local Psoriasis Severity Index scores relative to control plaques over 12 weeks (Pfaff et al. 2015).

A double-blind randomized comparative study of 20 participants tested blue 420-nm light against red 630-nm light. Both groups showed clinical improvement in treated plaques. Erythema continued to improve over the treatment course with blue light, whereas improvement with red light leveled off after the first six illuminations; scaling and induration did not show a comparable clear separation (Kleinpenning et al. 2012). Small uncontrolled reports of red or near-infrared LED treatment add observations but are not independent confirmation from large controlled populations.

Animal evidence

Two 2025 mouse studies reported reduced epidermal thickening and changes in inflammatory measures after red-light treatment in psoriasis-like models. One reported reductions in skin changes and some inflammatory markers, while not all systemic markers changed. These models help examine local skin effects but are not clinical psoriasis trials (Corrêa et al., 2025; Austin et al., 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Laboratory studies using keratinocyte or three-dimensional skin models report reduced proliferation or epidermal thickness under some red-light conditions. One experiment also used curcumin, so the light-only contribution cannot be separated.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical studies include blue visible light at 420 or 453 nm and red visible light at 630 nm. The mouse studies used red light near 640–660 nm. Reported fluences and irradiances differ substantially between studies, as do treatment frequency and duration. There is no head-to-head dose-finding program that identifies one best regimen. Results are local to treated plaques and should not be generalized to whole-body psoriasis or lasting remission.

Interpretation

The randomized studies found local improvement in treated plaques, with a wavelength-specific difference in the duration of erythema improvement in one small comparison. Red-light animal and laboratory studies report corresponding local skin changes. The clinical findings support short-term plaque improvement as a reasonable outcome to test further, but they do not show durable or systemic disease control.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term local plaque improvement with blue visible light Low for red-light benefit and durable disease control
Publications and records9 articles (one mapped psoriasis-like model)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small randomized within-person studies found improvement in treated plaques, including a comparison of blue and red light. This provides direct evidence for local, short-term outcomes, not whole-body disease control or lasting remission. Larger independent trials with common severity scores, treatment schedules, and follow-up after treatment stops would support broader conclusions and clarify whether results differ by wavelength.
